credit: Plates: a marginal drawing in the register of the Parlement of Paris (Archives nationales); three miniatures from Martial d'Auvergne's Vigiles de Charles VII and the armorial of the Berry herald (Bibliothèque nationale de France); a miniature from Christine de Pizan's own manuscript (British Library); the votive panel of the Jouvenel des Ursins family (Musée de Cluny); Jeanne's signature on a letter of 1430 and her letter to Riom in a facsimile of 1911; and pages of Quicherat's edition (1841–1849). Public-domain reproductions via Wikimedia Commons and the Internet Archive, resized for this site.
lede: The only image made in her lifetime, by a clerk who never saw her; the people around her as their own age painted them, Christine, Dunois, the family of the judge of 1456; the images of the generation after the nullity trial; her name in her own hand; and pages of the edition this site reads. There is no picture of her death. Each plate names its source; the caption points to the passage it belongs with.

plates.titel: The clerk of the Parlement draws the Maid
plates.caption: In the margin of the Parlement of Paris's register, against the entry for Tuesday 10 May 1429 that reports the fighting at Orléans, the clerk Clément de Fauquembergue drew a girl with long hair, a sword and a banner. He had never seen her; it is the only image made in her lifetime, by a man in English-held Paris who knew her only from report.
plates.source: Paris, Archives nationales, X1a 1481, fol. 12r (detail), 10 May 1429; via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.titel: 'Par leur pont qui fondit en Loire'
plates.caption: The taking of the Tourelles in Martial d'Auvergne's verse chronicle of Charles VII's reign, c. 1484: 'How the French raised the siege valiantly and entered Orléans'. The verses below say that many English were killed in the assault 'and the others were drowned by their bridge, which gave way into the Loire': the same account as the city's Journal, which Quicherat corrected from the town accounts (Orl. Tourelles [2]).
plates.source: Martial d'Auvergne, Les Vigiles de Charles VII, Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, ms. fr. 5054, fol. 57v, c. 1484; Gallica btv1b105380390/f126, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.caption: Christine de Pizan presents the collected volume of her works to Queen Isabeau of Bavaria, about 1410–1414, in the manuscript made in her own workshop. Isabeau was the mother of Charles VII; by the treaty of Troyes (1420) she and her husband disinherited him in favour of Henry V. Fifteen years after this picture, Christine greeted the son 'who fled from Paris' as king (Ditié [1]).
plates.source: Master of the Cité des Dames, Christine de Pizan, The Book of the Queen, London, British Library, Harley 4431, fol. 3r (detail), c. 1410–1414; via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.caption: Jeanne, dressed as a woman, is led to the king by two men of his household. Under the picture the verses of Martial d'Auvergne have her say 'Gentil roy, je vous meneray couronner à Rains'. Painted some fifty years after the event, for a poem written in praise of Charles VII after the nullity trial: the image of 1484 is already the image of the rehabilitation.
plates.source: Martial d'Auvergne, Les Vigiles de Charles VII, Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, ms. fr. 5054, fol. 55v, c. 1484; via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.caption: The name at the foot of her letter to the people of Reims, written from Sully on 16 March 1430. She could not write; the letters she sent were dictated, and she seems to have learned to sign her name in the last year of her freedom. At Rouen the abjuration of 24 May 1431 was signed, by the witnesses' account, with a cross or a mark.
plates.source: Letter to the inhabitants of Reims, 16 March 1430, family archives of Maleissye (reproduction); via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.caption: The letter of 9 November 1429 asking Riom for powder, saltpetre, sulphur, arrows and crossbows for the siege of La Charité, written by a clerk and signed 'Jehanne' below. Quicherat, who held the original, thought the cramped letters of the signature showed a guided hand (Letters [4]).
plates.source: Moulins, 9 November 1429, Archives municipales de Riom; facsimile in C. de Maleissye, Les Lettres de Jehanne d'Arc (Paris 1911); via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.caption: The capture before Compiègne in Martial d'Auvergne's verse chronicle, c. 1484. The rubric reads 'How the Maid was taken before Compiègne and sold to the English'; the verses below say that the Picard who took her handed her to Luxembourg, 'who sold her and handed her on to the English for ready money'. That is the sentence missing from Monstrelet, Luxembourg's own chronicler (Mon. [4]).
plates.source: Martial d'Auvergne, Les Vigiles de Charles VII, Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, ms. fr. 5054, fol. 70r, c. 1484; Gallica btv1b105380390/f151, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.caption: The page of Quicherat's edition where the Twelve Articles begin: 'And first, a certain woman says and affirms that when she was thirteen years old...'. The articles name her nowhere; they were sent to the consultors at Rouen and to the University of Paris as propositions to be judged, not as the words of a person (Art. Twelve [1]).
plates.source: J. Quicherat, Procès de condamnation, vol. I (Paris 1841), p. 328; Internet Archive, procsdecondam01joanuoft (public domain).

plates.caption: The end of the French abjuration in Quicherat's edition, with the record's note of how it was signed: 'Jehanne' and a cross. In her letters of 1430 a cross could mean, she had told the judges, that the opposite of what was written should be done (Art. Twelve, article VI, not carried here). What she signed at Saint-Ouen, and how, were questions for the witnesses of the nullity trial (Ouen Abjuration [2]).
plates.source: J. Quicherat, Procès de condamnation, vol. I (Paris 1841), p. 448; Internet Archive, procsdecondam01joanuoft (public domain).

plates.caption: The page of Quicherat's edition with Isambart de la Pierre's deposition of March 1450: the secular judge who passed no sentence, 'Do your duty', and her request that he fetch the cross from the nearest church and hold it before her eyes. This site carries no picture of her death (End Isambart [3]–[4]).
plates.source: J. Quicherat, Procès de condamnation et de réhabilitation, vol. II (Paris 1844), p. 6; Internet Archive, procsdecondam02joanuoft (public domain).

plates.caption: Jean, count of Dunois, on horseback with the arms of Orléans crossed by the bastard's bend, in the armorial of Gilles le Bouvier, Berry herald of Charles VII; the inscription calls him 'conte de Dunois, bastard d'Orléans, lieutenant general'. In 1456 he was the first witness heard at Orléans, and remembered her first words to him: 'En nom Dieu, the counsel of God our Lord is safer and wiser than yours' (Wit. 1429 [1]).
plates.source: Gilles le Bouvier, Armorial, Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, ms. fr. 4985, fol. 18v, 15th century; Gallica btv1b85285803/f44, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.caption: Jean Jouvenel des Ursins, who had followed Charles VII into exile in 1418 and presided over his Parlement at Poitiers, kneels in prayer with his wife and their children, about 1445–1449. One of the sons, Jean, was bishop of Beauvais after Cauchon and archbishop of Reims from 1449; as such he presided over the court that declared the first trial null (Null. [1]).
plates.source: Anonymous, The Jouvenel des Ursins family, c. 1445–1449, from the chapel of Saint-Remi in Notre-Dame de Paris; Paris, Musée de Cluny (Louvre RF 9618); photograph via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).
